terms.CI/CD pipeline: A pipeline is usually defined as code next to the application (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkinsfile) and modeled as a directed graph of jobs. Design goals: fast feedback (cheap checks first, caching, parallelism, under about ten minutes for pull requests), hermetic and reproducible builds, a single immutable artifact promoted across environments, and least-privilege credentials via OIDC rather than stored keys. Merge queues test queued changes against the latest main. Health is measured with the DORA metrics: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore. Supply-chain hardening adds SBOMs, signed artifacts and SLSA provenance, plus pinning third-party actions to commit SHAs.
terms.Canary release: A canary compares a new version against a concurrently running baseline on live traffic, typically ramping 1%, 5%, 25%, 50%, 100% with a bake time per step. Automated canary analysis evaluates metrics such as error rate, p99 latency and saturation with statistical tests and aborts on regression; tools include Argo Rollouts, Flagger and service-mesh traffic splitting. Pitfalls: too little traffic to detect a difference, comparing to historical data instead of a live baseline, and biased routing through sticky sessions. Unlike an A/B test, which measures product impact, a canary asks one question: is the new build safe? Database changes must stay backward compatible because both versions run together.
terms.Feature flag: Flags fall into types with different lifetimes: release flags (days to weeks, removed after rollout), experiment flags for A/B tests, operational kill switches kept long term, and permission flags for entitlements. Evaluation happens in the application via an SDK that caches rules from a flag service, so flag checks must be fast and fail safe with a sensible default if the service is unreachable. Targeting can use user ID hashing for stable percentage rollouts. Risks: combinatorial explosion of untested states, stale flags as technical debt (track owners and expiry), and inconsistent behavior across services. OpenFeature is a vendor-neutral standard API for flag evaluation.
terms.Test double: Gerard Meszaros named five kinds: dummy, stub, spy, mock and fake. The crucial distinction is state verification (assert on results, possibly using stubs) versus behavior verification (assert on interactions, using mocks or spies). Over-mocking couples tests to implementation, so refactors break tests while behavior is unchanged. Guidelines: mock at architectural boundaries you own, wrap third-party APIs in adapters, prefer fakes for complex dependencies like repositories, and verify fakes against the real thing with contract or integration tests. In Python, unittest.mock with autospec=True enforces real signatures; mocking the wrong import path (where the name is looked up, not where it is defined) is a classic bug.
terms.Test-driven development: Formalized by Kent Beck, TDD runs in very short cycles; techniques include 'fake it' (hardcode a return value), triangulation (add cases that force generalization) and keeping a test list of behaviors still to cover. Classicist TDD uses real collaborators; mockist (London school) TDD works outside-in with mocks to discover interfaces. Related practices: acceptance-test-driven development and BDD, which write executable specifications in domain language. Studies show mixed productivity effects but consistent gains in test coverage and design modularity. TDD is strongest for well-specified logic and bug fixes (reproduce the bug as a failing test first) and weaker for exploratory prototypes, where tests often follow the spike.
terms.Flaky test: Large studies of flaky tests find async waits, concurrency and test-order dependence are the leading causes, followed by resource leaks, network, time and randomness. Detection: rerun failures and record pass-on-retry as flaky, run tests in random order, and run suites repeatedly under stress or with parallelism. Management: quarantine to a non-blocking job with an owner and deadline, and track flake rate per test. Automatic retries keep pipelines green but can hide genuine race conditions in production code, so log every retry. Fixes include explicit condition waits, injected clocks, seeded randomness, per-test databases or transactions, dynamic ports and hermetic test environments.
terms.Service level objective: A good SLI is a ratio of good to valid events measured close to the user, e.g. at the load balancer: successful requests under 300 ms divided by all valid requests. SLOs are set per critical user journey over a rolling window of 28 or 30 days, based on what users need and on historical performance, not on 100%. Each additional nine cuts allowed downtime tenfold: 99.9% allows 43.2 minutes per 30 days, 99.99% about 4.3 minutes. Serial dependencies multiply: two 99.9% dependencies cap you near 99.8%. SLAs sit below SLOs and carry remedies such as service credits. The OpenSLO specification lets teams define SLOs as code.
terms.Error budget: Error budget equals (1 - SLO) times eligible events, so 99.9% over 10 million requests allows 10,000 failures. Burn rate measures consumption relative to the even pace that would exhaust it at window end; a burn rate of 14.4 spends 2% of a 30-day budget in one hour. The SRE workbook recommends multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerts: page on fast burns confirmed by a short window, ticket on slow burns. An error budget policy, agreed beforehand by product and engineering, defines consequences on exhaustion, such as release freezes except for fixes and mandatory postmortems. Planned maintenance and dependency failures still count, because users feel them.
terms.Distributed tracing: A trace is a directed tree of spans sharing a 128-bit trace ID; each span has a 64-bit span ID, parent ID, timing, attributes, events and status. W3C Trace Context standardizes propagation via the traceparent and tracestate headers, and baggage carries user-defined key-values. OpenTelemetry provides APIs, SDKs, auto-instrumentation, the OTLP protocol and the Collector for processing and export. Sampling strategy drives cost and usefulness: head sampling decides at the root (cheap, may miss rare errors), tail sampling decides after completion (keeps errors and slow traces, needs buffering). Async boundaries such as queues need explicit context injection, often using span links rather than parent-child relations.
terms.Infrastructure as code: Declarative IaC tools (Terraform, OpenTofu, CloudFormation, Bicep) keep a desired-state model and compute a plan as the diff between configuration, recorded state and reality; Pulumi and CDK generate the same kind of graph from general-purpose languages. Key concerns: remote state with locking, splitting state by blast radius, pinning provider and module versions, reviewing plans in pull requests, and applying only from CI with short-lived credentials. Drift detection runs plans on a schedule. Policy as code (Open Policy Agent, Sentinel) checks plans before apply. GitOps, with Argo CD or Flux, applies the same idea through continuous pull-based reconciliation, mostly for Kubernetes.
terms.Shared responsibility model: All major providers publish a shared responsibility model; the boundary shifts with the service model. For IaaS the customer handles guest OS patching, network configuration, IAM, encryption choices and data; for PaaS and managed databases the provider patches the platform; for SaaS the customer still owns identities, access configuration and data. Industry reports consistently attribute most cloud breaches to customer-side misconfiguration and credential compromise rather than provider failures. Compliance inheritance follows the same split: provider attestations such as SOC 2 cover only provider layers. Tools for the customer side include audit logging, posture management scanners, organization guardrails and customer-managed encryption keys.
terms.Least privilege: Least privilege applies to humans, services and CI systems alike. In AWS IAM, requests are denied by default, explicit Allows grant access, and explicit Denies always win; organization policies and permission boundaries cap the maximum. Practical techniques: start from minimal policies and expand using access logs or unused-permission analyzers, scope resources by ARN and conditions (tags, source network, MFA), avoid wildcards, use roles and workload identity federation instead of long-lived keys, and grant elevated access just in time with expiry. Watch for privilege escalation paths, such as permission to pass a powerful role to a new resource or to edit one's own policies.
